Updated CPU TAM Model Post Computex
A CPU, or a central processing unit, is a type of processor that functions as the 
“brains” of a system and is commonly found in servers, PCs, smartphones, and 
various IoT devices. The server CPU market has historically been one of the most 
competitive and profitable applications for CPUs. For example, Intel’s Data Center 
segment typically had operating margins north of 40% for most of the 2010’s. 
Server CPUs come in a variety of flavors, including different core counts, ISA’s 
(instruction set architecture), channel counts, and various other factors.

Prior to the explosion of agentic AI, a CPU was primarily limited to two main 
applications: 1.)  traditional workflows and 2.) acting as the head node for AI 
applications. In a head node, the CPU merely does the “management” by sending 
the user request to the GPU and sending the output back to the user. In this 
context, the GPU is doing heavy lifting such as running matrix multiplications to 
train LLMs or doing the inferencing when you query a chatbot. The third new 
application for CPUs is agentic AI, and this new application has seen explosive 
growth within the past year as AI has moved from chatbot inferencing to agentic
source_file: data/inputs/reports/AMD/2026-06-12-Citi-Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.O)_ GPU Upside Not Fully Priced-In; Upgrade to Buy w_$575 TP.pdf

text:

that are handling the orchestration, reasoning loops, data processing, and security 
components of autonomous AI agents. In Agentic AI, CPUs have become the new 
bottleneck as CPU-to-GPU ratios move from 1:8 in model training, to 1:4 in 
inferencing, to 1:1 or greater in agentic AI.
We believe AMD will be the primary beneficiary of the CPU renaissance due to their 
performance leadership, greater core counts, X86 ISA, broader SKU offerings, and 
support for both multithreading and single threading. In this framework, we
